The Birdwing pearlymussel (Lemiox rimosus) completes its larval metamorphosis following an obligatory parasitic phase on host fish, after which the newly metamorphosed juvenile emerges at a small total length of approximately 0.0254 cm [Lb = approximately 0.0254 cm], a figure borrowed from the closely related Actinonaias ligamentina in the absence of direct measurements for this species. Following settlement, the juvenile undergoes a prolonged period of somatic growth, with field surveys and mark-recapture studies indicating that individuals attain the adult shell length at a maximum of 5.2 cm [Li = 5.2 cm]. The growth trajectory is notably slow, a characteristic shared with other freshwater mussel species inhabiting stable, low-productivity lotic systems. This ultimate length is typically reached only after several years of steady accretion, with annual growth increments becoming markedly smaller as the individual approaches its asymptotic size. The species is predominantly found in clean, well-oxygenated riffles of medium-sized rivers, and its relatively modest maximum shell dimension is consistent with its life-history strategy as a long-lived, equilibrium species adapted to stable habitats.

The age at which Lemiox rimosus achieves sexual maturity has been estimated from histological examination of gonadal tissue across a size series of collected specimens. Puberty, defined by the onset of active gametogenesis, is consistently associated with a shell length of 2.5 cm [Lp = 2.5 cm], a threshold that individuals typically surpass during their third or fourth growing season. This size-based rather than strict age-based cue for reproductive maturation is common among freshwater bivalves, as it ensures that energetic investment in reproduction occurs only after a sufficiently large body frame has been established to support gamete production and brooding. Gravid females collected at or above this size threshold have been observed brooding glochidia in their marsupial demibranchs, confirming reproductive functionality. The attainment of this length marks a critical life-history transition, after which resources are partitioned between continued somatic growth and the production of offspring.

Detailed morphometric analyses and gravimetric measurements of adult Lemiox rimosus specimens have provided reliable estimates of maximum body mass. The ultimate wet weight, which includes both the shell and any environmental water retained within the mantle cavity, reaches 7.51 g [Wwi = 7.51 g] in the largest, most robust individuals. This value represents the asymptotic mass recorded from a population in the Duck River system, where habitat conditions are considered optimal. The wet weight tends to exhibit considerable individual variation, influenced by seasonal reproductive condition and microhabitat quality, but the upper bound of 7.51 g provides a benchmark for comparing body size among populations. When contrasted with related species like Actinonaias ligamentina, which achieve a substantially larger size, the relatively modest mass of Lemiox rimosus underscores its specialization for life in shallow, more hydrologically variable stream reaches where a heavier shell might be disadvantageous.

Longevity data for this species, derived from annual growth-ring counts on sectioned shells of individuals collected from known localities, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], as recorded under the thermal regime typical of its native habitat at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This extended lifespan places Lemiox rimosus among the longer-lived members of its freshwater mussel assemblage. The slow-paced life history, characterized by delayed maturation and low annual reproductive output, is a classic adaptation to the stable but resource-limited conditions of interior riverine environments. Seasonal temperature variation plays a crucial role in dictating metabolic rates and thus the rate of shell accretion that determines the ultimate expression of lifespan. The observed longevity is consistent with the low natural adult mortality rates inferred from population age structures, which show a high proportion of older individuals.

Comparisons of maximum shell length across several populations of Lemiox rimosus reveal that the ultimate total length of 5.2 cm [Li = 5.2 cm] appears to be a conservative trait, with variation of only a few millimeters among sites with differing flow regimes. The combination of a modest adult mass and a laterally compressed shell morphology provides an adaptive advantage for burrowing in stable, gravel-dominated substrates, reducing the energetic cost of vertical movement within the substratum, a frequent behavior linked to feeding and predator avoidance. The delayed attainment of its pubertal length of 2.5 cm [Lp = 2.5 cm] compared to more rapidly maturing species reinforces its characterization as a K-selected strategist. Together, these life-history traits—small size, slow growth, and considerable longevity—define its ecological role within its imperiled freshwater community.
